sections.title: What we are building
sections.body:
We are building a **single BBS platform** for Bahri, designed to support **1,500 observers** drawn from **4,000 crew members** across **107 vessels**. The programme is highly analytical at its core: every observation feeds deep analytics and fleet-wide insights, not just record-keeping.

### ICB form: familiar shape, Bahri-owned

The ICB form follows the same structure as Dekra, with everything , plus:

- **Unique account per observer:** personal identity, history, and accountability
- **Red Flag support:** immediate escalation from observer to office
- **Unique ICB numbering, feedback, and barriers:** searchable, auditable, explainable
- **Add or edit ICBS categories and vessel-specific operations:** mooring, cargo, pilot ladder, and more, configured by office

Mobile for crew and observers at sea. Web for shore office. Offline capture with auto sync when connectivity returns.

sections.title: Observer sign-on flow
sections.body:
An observer **cannot submit an observation** until they are assigned to a vessel. Assignment can happen in three ways:

1. **Observer-initiated:** the observer sends a sign-on request for a vessel; the vessel captain receives it by email and approves or declines
2. **Captain-initiated:** the vessel captain (vessel account) directly assigns a crew member to the vessel
3. **Office-initiated:** shore office assigns a crew member to a vessel from the admin panel

### Observers sign in

Observers sign in through one of three methods:

- **MIPS authentication gateway:** through MIPS using API integration
- **Email verification OTP:** standard one-time password flow
- **Authenticator app:** TOTP-based; works without internet once configured

flowchart TD

  Gate --> Req[Observer requests sign-on]
  Req --> Email[Captain receives email]
  Email --> Approve{Approved?}
  Approve -->|Yes| Assigned[Assigned to vessel]
  Approve -->|No| Blocked[Cannot observe]
  Gate --> Cap[Captain assigns crew member]
  Cap --> Assigned
  Gate --> Off[Office assigns to vessel]

sections.mermaidCaption: Three routes to vessel assignment, one gate before observation

sections.title: Observer perspective
sections.body:
When an observer first boards, they complete onboarding: profile details, rank, and a profile picture. From there, the observer hub gives them everything they need .

### What observers can do

- **Create an observation:** submit a full ICB form against their assigned vessel
- **View previous observations:** full personal history, searchable and filterable
- **Receive announcements:** fleet-wide or targeted broadcasts from office
- **Chat with office and vessel:** shared chatroom for follow-up, Red Flags, and coordination
- **Personal analysis:** charts and trends on their own observation patterns
- **Observation schedule:** monthly targets set by office (e.g. 5 observations required, 3 completed so far)
- **Vessel track record:** complete history of every vessel they have worked on, with full records per assignment

sections.mermaidCaption: Onboard once, then observe, communicate, and track progress from one place

sections.title: Vessel perspective
sections.body:
Vessels do **not** create observations. The vessel account is focused on crew management and visibility.

### Vessel responsibilities

- Maintain **vessel profile and particulars:** type, flag, fleet assignment
- **Sign on and sign off crew members:** approve observer requests or assign crew directly
- **Interactive chatroom:** chatroom between STO , ETS and Office
- **Optional observation preview:** administrators can enable or disable whether the vessel account can view observations created on that vessel

This keeps the vessel captain in control of who is on board, without adding observation overhead to the bridge.

sections.mermaidCaption: Crew management and optional observation visibility. No observation creation.

sections.title: Office member perspective
sections.body:
Office members are assigned as shore-side users and **do not require vessel sign-on** to create observations. They can observe during shore visits or fleet inspections without the captain approval flow.

### Everything an observer has, plus

- **Fleet overview:** preview their assigned fleet and vessel activity
- **Fleet analytics:** access to analysis and reporting across their scope

### Interaction module

A dedicated channel between **office administrators**, **STO**, and **ETS** for timely coordination on assigned vessels. Office can share what matters onboard without leaving the platform.

- **Focus areas:** set and communicate priority behaviours or operations for a vessel or fleet group
- **Inspection protocols:** publish and track protocols for upcoming inspections so shore and vessel stay aligned
- **Announcements and Red Flags:** surface fleet broadcasts and Red Flags raised onboard in one place, with context on the assigned vessel

This keeps administrators, STO, and ETS working from the same picture when something needs attention at sea.

### Authentication

Office members sign in via **Microsoft Single Sign-On**, integrated with Bahri's existing identity provider.

sections.title: Administrator perspective
sections.body:
Administrators previlidges to the platform: **user management**, **vessel management**, **crew oversight**, and the **analytics engine** that ties the entire programme together. This is the most important surface in the application.

### Deep analytics

- **Compare observers:** side-by-side performance, volume, and quality metrics across the fleet
- **Custom dashboards:** build, save, and **share** dashboards with other office users
- **Excel export:** full analysis export for offline review and reporting
- **ICB vs ICB analytics:** compare behaviour categories, trends, and patterns over time
- **Custom filters on request:** any dimension Bahri needs (vessel type, rank, route, operation) can be added as the programme matures

The analytics page is the core that links every part of the app. Observations in, insights out.

sections.title: Data migration and integration
sections.body:
To migrate from Dekra, we need a structured data handoff and a purpose-built ingestion pipeline.

### Process

1. **Extract** historical data from Dekra: observations, crew records, and configuration
2. **Analyse** the export to map fields, categories, and relationships to the new schema
3. **Build** a data ingestion pipeline that loads validated records into the Bahri platform
4. **Verify** migrated data against Dekra totals before go-live

### Data required from Bahri / Dekra

- **Observation data:** full historical ICB records from Dekra
- **Crew member list:** all Bahri crew with observer status flagged for each user

Once ingested, historical observations feed the same analytics engine as new submissions. No gap in reporting continuity.
sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  Dekra[Dekra export] --> Analyse[Data analysis]
  Analyse --> Pipeline[Ingestion pipeline]
  Pipeline --> Validate[Validation]
  Validate --> Platform[Bahri BBS platform]
  Platform --> Analytics[Analytics engine]
sections.mermaidCaption: Extract, map, ingest, verify. Continuous reporting from day one.

sections.title: Delivery timeline
sections.body:
The platform will be **fully built and production-ready in three intensive development months**, targeting **1 November 2026** as the go-live date.

Development runs in focused milestones with **review loops between TailoredTech and Mr Joseph** (Bahri) after each phase, refining features until the product meets operational requirements.

### Milestones

| Phase | Window | Deliverable |
|-------|--------|-------------|
| **M1: Core** | Month 1 (Aug 2026) | Auth, roles, ICB form, vessel and crew management, basic observations |
| **M2: Operations** | Month 2 (Sep 2026) | Sign-on flows, observer tools, chat, announcements, schedules, offline sync |
| **M3: Analytics** | Month 3 (Oct 2026) | Admin dashboards, deep analytics, custom filters, Excel export, data migration pipeline |
| **Go-live** | 1 Nov 2026 | Production launch across fleet |
| **Iteration** | Post-launch | Loop sessions with Mr Joseph, enhancements until final production sign-off |

page.headline: Out of
page.tagline: OOP sits inside Bahri's Approval module — the same family as MOC and PCR. In-house control for vessel and shore, multi-organization IDs, sequential approval chains, and operational close-out that Teams policy cannot deliver.

sections.title: OOP inside the Approval module
sections.body:
Out of Policy is not a standalone tool. It is a **first-class workflow inside Bahri's Approval module** — the same platform family that already carries **MOC** and **PCR**.

That matters operationally: one identity model, one request language, one audit posture. OOP inherits the approval DNA of management of change and procedure change, then specializes it for controlled deviations from policy.

### Why this belongs with MOC & PCR

- **Shared approval DNA:** levels, ownership, notifications, and close-out patterns stay consistent across change and deviation work
- **One governance surface:** shore and vessel users learn one module family, not three disconnected tools
- **Clear ownership:** Bahri-owned, in-house delivery — not an outsourced Teams policy bolted on the side

OOP answers a simple question with enterprise rigor: *when policy must be temporarily exceeded, who authorized it, under what conditions, and what was the operational outcome?*

sections.title: Vessel and office initiation
sections.body:
Policy deviations do not only start on shore. The Approval OOP workflow supports **initiation from vessel and from office**, so operational reality is captured where it happens.

### What this unlocks

- **Vessel-led requests:** bridge and technical teams raise OOP with vessel context, attachments, and risk assessment already in the record
- **Office-led requests:** shore teams initiate when the deviation is planned from land or coordinated across the fleet
- **Shared lifecycle:** wherever it starts, the same sequential approval, tracking, and close-out apply

Teams OOP policy does not support this dual initiation model. That gap forces workarounds — email, parallel chats, or incomplete records when the event begins at sea.
bullets: Mandatory vessel and location fields on every request
Same approval chain whether raised onboard or ashore
Operational titles tied to vessel identity in the tracking list

sections.title: Multiple organization support
sections.body:
Bahri operations span organizational boundaries. OOP request IDs and governance are built for **multiple organizations** — visible in serialized prefixes such as organization-scoped OOP numbers in the tracking list.

### Why multi-org matters

- **Clear ownership:** each request carries organization context in its identity, not buried in free text
- **Filterable scope:** lists, printouts, and follow-ups can be governed by organization without splitting into separate tools
- **Enterprise readiness:** Teams OOP policy does not support multi-organization structure at this level

This is foundational for an Approval module that must scale across Bahri entities without losing audit clarity.
bullets: Organization-aware request serialization
Tracking list visibility across org-scoped IDs
Aligned with the wider Approval module architecture

sections.title: Sequential approval
sections.body:
OOP approvals are **ordered by design**. Approvers are arranged in levels — reorderable, extendable, and visible on every request — so authorization is a chain, not a flat chat reaction.

### How the chain works

- **Configurable levels:** add, remove, and reorder approvers before initiation
- **Role-aware assignment:** VP, President, and supporting roles appear in sequence with clear accountability
- **Progress in the list:** tracking shows who has already approved and who is next
- **Close-out awareness:** the user handling close-out is notified after follow-up automatically

Teams OOP policy does not support hierarchy / sequential approval. That is one of the clearest capability gaps versus the in-house Approval module.
bullets: Numbered approval levels with up/down reordering
Initiate OOP only when the chain is defined
Approver progress visible as checkmarks in the tracking list

sections.mermaidCaption: Ordered levels before initiation — then operational follow-up

sections.title: Request intake and required documents
sections.body:
Every OOP starts as a structured request: title, vessel, location, event description, and mandatory risk documentation.

### Built for compliance, not free-form chat

- **Rich description:** formatted narrative of the out-of-policy event
- **Risk assessment:** mandatory upload — not optional context
- **Required documents:** experience, drawings, and action plan called out at intake
- **Attachments:** PDF, images, Word, Excel, and more in one evidence pack

Teams policy does not identify required documents or keep uploaded evidence viewable in a proper request log. The Approval OOP form closes that gap at the front door.
bullets: Mandatory title, vessel, and location
Risk assessment document required
Supporting attachments guided at creation

sections.title: Tracking, reminders, and printouts
sections.body:
Once live, OOP is managed from a **tracking list** with search, status, experience outcome, timestamps, approver progress, and attachments.

### Governance surfaces

- **Statuses:** Requested, Approved — Follow up, Closed, Declined, Cancelled
- **Experience tags:** Safely, Potential hazard / red flag, Cancelled
- **Filters:** request scope, experience, titles, types, and date range
- **Reminders:** follow-up prompts so approved deviations do not go silent
- **Printouts:** request printout plus filtered Excel / PDF log export

Where Teams is basic or limited, the Approval module gives operators a real control room for OOP — not a message thread pretending to be a register.
bullets: Searchable multi-filter tracking list
Reminder follow-up on open commitments
Printout request and filtered Excel + PDF log

images.label: OOP tracking list · status and approvers

sections.title: Follow-up on OOP event
sections.body:
Approval is not the end of the story. **Follow-up on the OOP event** records the operational experience outcome — marked crucial in the capability gap analysis because Teams does not support it.

### Close the loop

- **Cancelled:** the event did not materialise after approval
- **Safely:** completed without concerns, with required justification
- **Potential hazard / red flag:** hazard observed, captured for learning and escalation
- **Optional attachments:** photos, reports, or supporting documents on the follow-up itself

This turns OOP from a permission slip into an **operational learning record** — the same seriousness MOC and PCR expect after change is executed.
bullets: Experience outcome required on follow-up
Justification captured against the selected outcome
Close-out handler notified after follow-up

sections.title: What Teams cannot carry
sections.body:
Teams OOP policy covers a thin slice: tracking list, reminders, and basic printout. The Approval module OOP is built for the full control loop.

### Gaps closed by the in-house module

- No multi-org model
- No sequential / hierarchy approval
- No vessel and office initiation
- No cloning, close-out, or transition chatroom
- No required-document identification or document viewing in log
- No proper audit log
- No follow-up on OOP event
- Limited filtering and printout log options
- Out-of-organization access constrained to Teams users

Keeping OOP inside the **Approval module** means Bahri owns the workflow, the data, and the roadmap — alongside MOC and PCR — instead of stretching a collaboration tool into a compliance system.

sections.title: Roadmap · generic approval and DOC sign
sections.body:
OOP is the next proof point that the Approval module is a **platform**, not a one-off form.

### Near-term direction

- **Generic approval module:** reuse the sequential chain, tracking, notifications, and close-out patterns beyond OOP / MOC / PCR — so new approval types inherit the same spine
- **DOC sign:** extend the approval and evidence model toward controlled document signing, keeping identity, audit, and attachment discipline intact

### Strategic read

Every OOP request that runs through vessel/office initiation, multi-org identity, and sequential levels strengthens the case for a Bahri-owned approval fabric. The product already in MOC and PCR grows into a broader authorization layer — with OOP as a live, operational demonstration.
bullets: OOP proves Approval module patterns in production use
Generic approval reuses the same chain and close-out DNA
DOC sign planned as the next controlled-evidence capability
